tagline: From Potomac crossings to mountain passes, a campaign route reaches Sharpsburg.
intro: The Antietam Campaign Scenic Byway links White’s Ferry on the Potomac with Sharpsburg, passing through Poolesville, Frederick and South Mountain. Maryland’s tourism office presents it as a journey through Civil War sites and Western Maryland landscapes, listing 126 miles and three to four hours of driving. The route brings together river country, battlefields and a mountain crossing, with trails at Monocacy and South Mountain offering places to leave the car.

In September 1862, Robert E. Lee moved his Confederate army into Maryland, seeking a victory on Union soil that would win foreign support. Fighting at South Mountain preceded the September 17 battle near Antietam Creek. Lincoln issued his preliminary Emancipation Proclamation on September 22, but it did not free enslaved Marylanders: Maryland was not in rebellion. A new state constitution ended slavery there in 1864.

Drive from White’s Ferry through Poolesville toward Monocacy National Battlefield and Frederick. Frederick’s National Museum of Civil War Medicine explores medical innovation during the war. Continue west beyond Braddock Heights, then toward South Mountain; Washington Monument State Park offers a walk to its stone tower. The byway continues through Boonsboro to the Antietam battlefield and Sharpsburg, where Tolson’s Chapel adds the history of a Black congregation and its school to the campaign story.

moments.title: Poolesville
moments.text: The settlement itself grew from a log store John Poole Jr. built in 1793, on land inherited from his father. The Potomac’s shallow fords made Poolesville a place to watch the river during the Civil War. Union soldiers were stationed near the water to monitor Confederate incursions into Maryland, and troops assembled here before crossing into Virginia for the Battle of Ball’s Bluff in 1861. Confederate horsemen passed through in 1863 on their way to Gettysburg. The town’s wartime role can be explored through Civil War exhibits in the John Poole House, which Maryland’s tourism office dates to circa 1793.

moments.title: Washington Monument State Park
moments.text: Boonsboro’s citizens began their monument to George Washington with a march from the town square on July 4, 1827. They raised a dry-laid stone tower to 15 feet that day; workmen returned later in the year to bring it to 30 feet. The original became the first completed monument dedicated to Washington, but weather and vandalism reduced it to rubble. During the Civil War, the Union Army used the ruined monument as a signal station. The tower’s present form is a Civilian Conservation Corps reconstruction, dedicated in 1936, beside the Appalachian Trail near South Mountain’s summit.

moments.title: Tolson's Chapel
moments.text: Blackboards survive on the side walls of Tolson’s Chapel, a reminder that this church also served as a school. Local African Americans built it in 1866 on land given by Samuel Craig, a free Black man. In 1868, the Freedmen’s Bureau funded teachers for a short period. After Maryland required school districts to provide schools for African Americans in 1872, the chapel again became a schoolhouse, serving that role until 1899. Its log structure is finished with board-and-batten siding and topped by a square belfry. Inside, pews flank a single aisle, and a raised dais and pulpit occupy the far end of the room.

practical: Poolesville: The cached account lists White’s Ferry as inactive, with operations suspended in 2020; it does not establish a usable Potomac crossing. (checked 2026-10-11)
